title: Plotting to understand, not to present
story:
One word covers two jobs, and the standards that make a plot good at one make it bad at the other.

The first job is finding out what is in the data. Its audience is you, its lifetime is ten minutes, and its quality measure is how many questions you got through. Plots for this should be fast, ugly and numerous — no titles, no palette, no alignment, nothing that costs time and adds no information. The failure mode here is polish: an hour spent making one chart presentable is an hour not spent looking at the other twenty columns.

The second job is convincing somebody of a conclusion you have already reached. Its audience is a reader who will give it a few seconds and cannot ask you anything. Now every choice matters, because the reader's understanding is limited by what their visual system can decode.

And that is measurable rather than a matter of taste. Cleveland and McGill identified the elementary perceptual tasks people carry out when pulling quantitative information out of a graph, and ranked them by the accuracy of the resulting judgements — position along a common scale first, then position along non-aligned scales, then length, direction and angle, then area, then volume and curvature, and last shading and colour saturation. The ordering came from ten common graph types with formal experiments on about fifty subjects. So encoding a quantity as an angle rather than as a position is a decision with a known cost, and the reason a bar chart usually beats a pie chart is that one asks the reader to compare positions along a common scale and the other asks them to compare angles.

Two cautions keep this from becoming a rule to recite. The authors themselves warned against the conceptual trap of adopting accuracy as the sole criterion — a graph also has to be read at all, and their design principle is stated comparatively, about two forms conveying the same information. And the ranking tells you about decoding a value, not about whether the plot was worth making.

For the first job, the demonstration to keep in mind is from 2017. Matejka and Fitzmaurice gave a method for generating data sets identical across a chosen set of statistical properties yet producing entirely dissimilar graphs, by perturbing individual points from a seed data set under simulated annealing — notably agnostic about which properties are held fixed, so the trick is not a quirk of one statistic. Their dinosaur-shaped seed came from Alberto Cairo. The moral is not that statistics lie. It is that a fixed set of summaries cannot constrain a shape, which is exactly why the first job exists and why it comes first.

problem.name: Graphical perception
problem.shape: A picture has to be made of some numbers, and it is about to be used either to find something out or to convince someone — which are different jobs with opposite standards.
tell: an exploratory plot is being tidied up for an audience
a chart is going to a reader who cannot ask a question about it
quantities are encoded as angles, areas or colour intensity
the categories are unsorted and the reader is expected to rank them
problem.move: Decide which job you are doing before you make the picture. To find things out, make plots fast, plain and many, and throw them away. To convince, pick the encoding from the ranking — position along a common scale before length or angle, and angle before area or shading — then sort the categories so comparison becomes a matter of adjacent positions, and label it for a reader who cannot ask you anything.
problem.invariant: The reader's understanding is bounded by what their visual system can decode, and the accuracy of that decoding depends on the channel the quantity was encoded in. The ranking of those channels is an experimental result about people rather than a matter of preference.
problem.breaks: The ranking concerns decoding a single value accurately, and accuracy is not the only criterion — its own authors warned against that trap, and the principle was stated as a comparison between two forms carrying the same information. A more accurate encoding that the audience will not read, or that answers a question nobody asked, is not the better chart.

cost.time: the presenting plot is slow by nature, which is the argument for not spending that time on the exploratory ones
cost.beats: shipping an exploratory plot to a reader, which saves the work of choosing an encoding and transfers the decoding problem to someone with no access to the data and no way to ask

worked.problem: Why is a pie chart usually worse than a bar chart, and when is it not?
worked.reasoning:
Because the two charts ask the reader's visual system to do different work, and one of those tasks is measurably more accurate than the other.

The ranking of elementary perceptual tasks puts position along a common scale at the top and length, direction and angle several places below it. A bar chart encodes each quantity as a position along a shared axis; a pie chart encodes it as an angle, and the segments have no common baseline to be read against. So for the job of recovering values and comparing them, the bar chart is using the more accurate channel, and that is an experimental finding about people rather than a stylistic preference.

The effect compounds with the number of categories. Comparing two angles of similar size is hard, ordering eight of them is harder, and a reader trying to rank the slices is performing the least reliable version of the task repeatedly.

Where the pie is not worse is where the question is different. The criterion its authors set out is comparative — one form is preferable to another form conveying the same quantitative information — and they explicitly warned against the conceptual trap of treating accuracy as the sole criterion. If the reader's question is part-to-whole with two or three categories, and the answer needed is roughly a half or roughly a quarter rather than a value, then a pie communicates the whole directly, the judgement is coarse enough for angle to serve, and it is legible to an audience that reads it without instruction.

So my answer is that the choice follows the question. Recovering or ranking values, especially across many categories: a bar chart, and preferably sorted, since ordering makes the comparison a matter of adjacent positions. Conveying that a handful of parts make up a whole: a pie can be defended.

What I would not do is treat the ranking as a prohibition. It is a statement about the accuracy of decoding one value, it was formulated as a comparison between forms carrying the same information, and its own authors said accuracy is not the only thing that matters.

problem.practice: Take your last presented chart and name the perceptual task it asks of the reader, then check where that task sits in the ranking and whether a higher one would have carried the same information. Separately, take twenty columns you have never plotted and plot them all in one sitting with no titles, no colours and no tidying, and notice how much you learn against how long it took.

beats.broke: One word covers two jobs — finding out what is in the data, and convincing a reader of a conclusion — and the standards that make a plot good at one make it bad at the other.
beats.fix: Separate them deliberately. Disposable, plain, numerous plots while you are still finding out; one deliberately encoded and labelled plot once you know what the claim is and who has to read it.
beats.cost: The presenting job requires choosing an encoding, and encodings have a measured ranking by decoding accuracy — position along a common scale above length and angle, and those above area, volume and shading — which is a finding about people rather than a matter of taste.

interview.q: Why is a pie chart usually worse than a bar chart, and when is it not?
interview.trap: Reciting the ranking as a prohibition. It describes the accuracy of decoding one value, it was formulated as a comparison between forms conveying the same information, and the authors who established it warned against treating accuracy as the only criterion.
interview.answer:
Because the two charts ask the reader's visual system for different work, and one of those tasks is measurably more accurate.

The ranking of elementary perceptual tasks puts position along a common scale at the top, with length, direction and angle several places below. A bar chart encodes each quantity as a position on a shared axis. A pie encodes it as an angle, and its segments have no common baseline to be read against. So for recovering and comparing values the bar chart uses the more accurate channel — an experimental finding about people, not a stylistic preference.

It compounds with the number of categories: comparing two similar angles is hard, and ranking eight of them is the least reliable version of the task performed repeatedly.

Where the pie is not worse is where the question changes. The principle was stated comparatively — one form against another conveying the same information — and the authors explicitly warned against the conceptual trap of treating accuracy as the sole criterion. If the reader's question is part-to-whole across two or three categories, and the answer wanted is about a quarter rather than a number, then the pie shows the whole directly, the judgement is coarse enough for angle to carry it, and it is read without instruction by audiences who would need a moment with an axis.

So the choice follows the question. To recover or rank values, especially across many categories, a bar chart, and sorted if possible, because ordering turns the comparison into adjacent positions. To show that a few parts make up a whole, a pie is defensible.

What I would avoid is reciting the ranking as a prohibition. It concerns the accuracy of decoding a single value, it was formulated as a comparison between forms carrying the same information, and the people who established it said accuracy is not the only criterion.

takeaway: Plots to understand should be fast, plain and thrown away, while plots to present are bounded by what a reader's visual system can decode — and that decoding has a measured ranking, with position along a common scale above angle, which is the whole case against the pie chart and the reason it is not a prohibition.
